anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Query Plan Selection Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read or manipulate more data, rows, or time than the business need truly requires.
Query Plan Selection Anomaly : The optimizer chooses or reuses a substantially sub-optimal execution plan even though statistics are adequate, leading to inefficient access paths or join strategies.

When both flaws appear at once, the workload issues written at the application layer are executed through a plan that is already inefficient, creating a multiplicative performance penalty. Observable effects include: extreme and unpredictable statement latency spikes; the same SQL text showing wildly different runtimes across executions; transactions holding locks far beyond user think-time; CPU spikes, buffer-cache churn, and temp-space explosions as full-table or Cartesian scans iterate over bloated predicate sets; rapid oscillation between time-outs and apparent normalcy as bind-sensitive plans flip while the underlying query text remains logically bloated; and an unusual mix of application-side retries and optimizer-related plan cache growth.

Causally, ill-written SQL increases row counts, widens projections, or keeps transactions open, thereby enlarging the search space the optimizer must cost. This raises the probability that the cost model misjudges join orders, access paths, or degree of parallelism, producing a poor plan. Conversely, once a bad plan is chosen, its inefficiencies magnify the excess work mandated by the workload logic—e.g., a full scan on a table already over-read by non-sargable predicates—further stretching lock durations and resource usage. The two root causes therefore reinforce each other: workload logic bloats the operational footprint, while plan selection defects prevent the engine from mitigating that bloat, together degrading both OLTP and analytical performance.

entry.official_definition: Sets the interval between optional checks that the client is still connected while running queries.
entry.trigger_condition: During a long-running query, PostgreSQL polls the socket at this interval and can detect a closed connection sooner.
entry.workload_impact: Long-running queries can be aborted sooner after the kernel reports that the client connection is closed.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, disabling connection checks.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
